articles.title: Accused NC killer mom plans insanity defense — as retired judge says more may follow Lindsay Clancy strategy
articles.summary: Andrea Faust's insanity defense in her son's killing draws direct parallels to Lindsay Clancy's postpartum psychosis case as jurors deliberate.
articles.body: The insanity defense planned by a North Carolina mother accused of killing her son has drawn parallels to Lindsay Clancy’s trial and raised questions about whether it could become prevalent in criminal cases. Andrea Faust, 41, is charged with murder and attempted murder in the Feb. 12 death of her 3-year-old son and the attempted murder of her 2-year-old son at their home in Durham, North Carolina. Her attorneys have filed notice that they intend to rely on defenses of not guilty by reason of insanity and diminished capacity, WRAL reported. The case is drawing parallels to Clancy’s Massachusetts trial. Retired Massachusetts Superior Judge Jack Lu said he expects similar defenses to be raised more often as the Clancy case draws national attention to postpartum mental-health conditions. LINDSAY CLANCY DIDN'T SHOW 'BREAK WITH REALITY' AS JURY WEIGHS PSYCHOSIS DEFENSE: SUSAN SMITH PROSECUTOR Clancy has pleaded not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility in the 2023 deaths of her three children. Her defense argued she suffered from postpartum psychosis, while prosecutors argue she understood her actions and acted deliberately. Jurors ended a second day of deliberations Friday without reaching a verdict. They will return on Monday morning to continue working toward a verdict. In Faust’s case, the filing does not establish that she was legally insane or had diminished capacity. Her attorney, Nicole Galinsky, told the local outlet that a defense expert concluded Faust could not distinguish right from wrong during the alleged murders. "Andrea and Lindsay’s cases are eerily similar, though not entirely the same," Galinsky told Fox News Digital. Galinsky noted that Faust was not suffering from postpartum psychosis. "However, both women were known to be loving, doting, responsible mothers who were worried about and caring for their children up until the very second they decided to kill them," Galinsky said, adding that Faust and Clancy were both struggling with similar issues, including hallucinations, hospitalizations and mental health. "Neither woman did this out of the blue," Galinsky said in an email. "Both were struggling enormously with their mental health. But, like most women and almost all moms, they were just trying to get through each day, care for their children, be a good mom/wife/employee. Both were seeking help from doctors who weren’t really taking their concerns seriously. "Both of these cases highlight the failure in our society to take women and mothers seriously when it comes to their mental health. Both of these women advocated for themselves countless times and—for what? It got them nowhere. "I am hopeful that our case will demonstrate how to properly treat and rehabilitate a woman living her own worst nightmare. Lindsay Clancy was not given that luxury." FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X Lu said society and the legal system have not fully understood the effects postpartum mental illness can have on behavior and criminal responsibility. "Most of the time, these criminal responsibility, insanity, mental health defenses are unsuccessful," Lu told Fox News Digital. SEND US A TIP Faust was found incapable of proceeding to trial in March after court records documented serious concerns about her mental health and safety, according to WRAL. GOT A TIP? articles.body:
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul is travelling to northern Africa on Monday, with stops planned in Tunisia and Algeria.

A ministry spokesman said on Sunday that the two countries are important partners for Germany and Europe, acting as a bridge between the European and African continents.

In Tunis, Wadephul plans to meet his counterpart Mohamed Nafti before talks with business representatives and a visit to a start-up. He is to be accompanied by a business delegation.

Later in the afternoon, Wadephul intends to travel on to Algiers, where meetings are planned with Foreign Minister Ahmed Attaf and business representatives. He is also due to be received by President Abdelmadjid Tebboune.

The ministry spokesman said there is great potential to strengthen cooperation between the two countries and Europe, particularly in the field of renewable energy.

Regional issues such as the situation in the Middle East and the Sahel region are also set to be discussed.

articles.title: Parents of seriously ill children should get paid leave, says commissioner
articles.summary: Children's commissioner Dame Rachel de Souza has backed called for more support for parents and carers.
articles.body:
Parents of children with serious illnesses or disabilities should be entitled to paid leave from work, the children's commissioner Dame Rachel de Souza has said.

She called on the government to introduce a legal right to 12 weeks of paid leave at 90% of normal pay in order to lift the "immense pressure" and lost earnings families face when a child develops a debilitating condition.

Her intervention came as the government continued to consult on how to financially support families and unpaid carers looking after ill children in England, Scotland and Wales.

She said: "Parents should not be forced to choose between being at their seriously ill child's bedside and keeping their job."

Dame Rachel said that parents have told her of the "impossible choices" they have made when "splitting time between caring for their seriously ill and disabled children and trying to hold down a job".

She has also backed a "right to return to work" following extended periods of leave, saying it could help "families whose children have complex or fluctuating needs to remain in employment while providing the care their children need".

Dame Rachel called unpaid carer's leave to be increased from five to 10 days a year, and for the introduction of a form of paid carer's leave.

It comes after campaigning by the parents of Hugh Menai-Davis, who died of cancer aged six in 2021.

His parents Frances and Ceri Menai-Davis have advocated for a change to employment law that would require employers to guarantee three months' salaries to parents whose child faces serious physical or mental illness.

"There's no specific right that allows the parents to legally be by the bedside of the child in hospital," Ceri Menai-Davis said in June.

"If you're a parent with a child, there is nowhere else you are going to be other than their bedside."

A consultation on reforms to the support available to families and carers is due to close on Monday.

Kate Dearden, minister for the future of work, said: "Serious childhood illness is a heartbreaking situation for families.

"I've been incredibly moved by the powerful stories we have heard, and we will move quickly to consider how we can strengthen support and employment rights for families facing serious childhood illness."

articles.title: Russia, China leaders to meet at Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit
articles.summary: The organisation is not officially anti-West, but Russian and Chinese leaders have used it to amplify their worldview.
articles.body:
Russia’s Vladimir Putin, China’s Xi Jinping and more than a dozen other leaders are set to gather in Kyrgyzstan on Monday for the annual summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO).

The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation has historically focused on economic issues, but President Putin and President Xi have also used the summit to promote their vision of a multipolar world and to present a united front against the West.

The SCO’s founding declaration says the group is “not an alliance directed against other states”. However, at last year’s gathering, Putin accused Western countries of provoking the Ukraine war, while Xi denounced “acts of intimidation”, referring to US-Chinese tensions.

Also expected to be in attendance are Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and his Turkish counterpart Recep Tayyip Erdogan, though Turkiye is not a member of the organisation.

Pezeshkian is expected to hold bilateral talks with Putin at this year’s SCO in the Kyrgyz capital of Bishkek. The foreign ministers of both countries met in July during the SCO’s Council of Foreign Ministers meeting.

Iran joined the bloc in 2023 and maintains close military ties to Russia and energy links with China.

Alongside the SCO’s 10 permanent members, another 15 states are connected as “dialogue partners”, including Turkiye, Saudi Arabia and Qatar.

The leaders of India and Pakistan, both of which are full members of the SCO, are also expected to attend.

The bloc claims to represent some 40 percent of the world’s population and 25 percent of global GDP. This year marks 25 years since the SCO was founded.

The meeting comes shortly after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he would encourage G20 members to re-examine terms of trade with China, denouncing Beijing’s $1.2 trillion global trade surplus as unsustainable.

“The world cannot have a China with a US$1.2 trillion (HK$9.36 trillion) trade surplus,” Bessent told the Reuters news agency on Sunday, ahead of a G20 finance leaders meeting in the United States.

“In China, the economy is quite weak, and they are trying to export their way out of it, and they need to rebalance their economy,” he added.

The US Treasury chief also said that he planned to hold a bilateral meeting during the G20 conference with People’s Bank of China Governor Pan Gongsheng, but declined to discuss details.

Subsequently, the suspects suddenly swerved their vehicle to the right, towards this area," Narendra Pratap Singh said.Speaking to ANI, ADG Law and Order (Uttar Pradesh) Amitabh Yash further detailed the ongoing police operation and the recovery of illicit firearms from the individuals."Ankit Baliyan was murdered near the Shamli Kotwali. articles.title: Karina becomes major Cat. 3 hurricane in Pacific Ocean
articles.summary: Karina rapidly strengthened into a major Category 3 hurricane Sunday evening and was moving west over the Pacific Ocean, forecasters said.
articles.body:
Aug. 30 (UPI) -- Karina rapidly strengthened into a major Category 3 hurricane Sunday evening and was moving west over the Pacific Ocean, forecasters said.

The hurricane had maximum sustained winds of 125 mph and was located about 960 miles west-southwest of the southern tip of Baja California in northwestern Mexico, the National Hurricane Center said in its 5 p.m. PDT update .

It was moving west at 9 mph. Hurricane-force winds extend outward up to 5 miles, according to the NHC.

Forecasters said the storm is expected to take a slower westward to west-northwest motion over the next few days, with some additional strengthening possible.

Swells generated by the storm are forecast to affect the coast of southwest Mexico and the Baja California Peninsula during that time, according to the NHC, which warned that they are likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions.

articles.title: In 1940, actor James Cagney bought hundreds of acres of California grassland; decades later the remaining 417 acres became a protected wildlife corridor
articles.summary: US News: For decades, the grasslands outside Ramona, California, looked much as they had for generations: open country, seasonal pools and wide stretches of na.
articles.body: For decades, the grasslands outside Ramona, California, looked much as they had for generations: open country, seasonal pools and wide stretches of native vegetation broken by grazing land. As reported by the local news report, The San Diego Union-Tribune, among the people who once owned part of this landscape was Hollywood actor James Cagney, who acquired hundreds of acres in the area with his brother William during the 1940s. The property did not remain intact forever. Portions were sold over the years, leaving 417 acres under the William J. Cagney Trust.By the early 2000s, however, the remaining tract had caught the attention of conservationists for a very different reason. It was part of one of the last sizable grassland habitats in coastal Southern California, supporting rare plants and threatened wildlife. In 2003, after years of negotiations, the Nature Conservancy purchased the former Cagney property for $2.7 million, placing the remaining land on a path toward long-term protection.How the Cagney brothers acquired the Ramona grasslands in the 1940sRamona was a very different place when the Cagney brothers acquired their land. The community was still relatively rural, and the grasslands stretched across a wide valley floor. The property was used as open country, with livestock grazing among native grasses and seasonal wetlands.Reportedly, James Cagney was already a major film star by this period, known for films such as The Public Enemy and Yankee Doodle Dandy. His brother William, however, had a separate connection to the property and remained associated with the Ramona holding.Accounts of the land differ slightly on the exact size of the original purchase, but later reporting put it at more than 500 acres. Over the following decades, portions were sold. What remained became the Cagney Ranch, held through the family trust.As reported, by the time conservation groups began seriously pursuing the property, the 417-acre remnant had become more significant than its size alone suggested.How the Ramona grasslands kept habitats connectedLarge grassland valleys are not easy to preserve in coastal Southern California. Their flat terrain makes them attractive for roads, houses and other development, leaving relatively few expansive areas intact.The Ramona grasslands were one of those exceptions. The wider area covered thousands of acres and contained a mixture of grassland, vernal pools and other habitats. It also formed part of a larger network of open land extending through San Diego County. Conservation groups saw the remaining large parcels as opportunities to keep those connections intact rather than allowing the landscape to become increasingly fragmented.The Cagney property sat close to the centre of that effort. It was not an isolated patch of vegetation surrounded by development. Its position meant that protecting it could help connect other conservation areas and leave room for further acquisitions.Rare wildlife found across the Ramona grasslandsThe land also supported species that had become increasingly difficult to find elsewhere.The Nature Conservancy identified the Stephens' kangaroo rat, San Diego fairy shrimp and arroyo southwestern toad among the threatened or endangered species associated with the Ramona grasslands. Seasonal vernal pools on the Cagney property had also produced records of three rare plant species.Vernal pools are particularly distinctive features of the landscape. They fill during the wet season and then dry out, creating temporary aquatic habitats that can support species adapted to conditions found in few other places.For conservationists, preserving the surrounding grassland mattered as well. Wildlife does not necessarily remain inside the boundaries of a single protected parcel. Maintaining open ground between habitats can allow animals and plants to persist across a wider landscape.How the Ramona grasslands deal took six years to completeThe Nature Conservancy did not simply arrive one day and purchase the ranch. The idea had been developing for years.Dave Bittner, executive director of the Wildlife Research Institute in Ramona, had first contacted the conservancy about the property in 1997. Discussions continued, and the acquisition began taking clearer shape around 2000.That long timeline was typical of large conservation purchases. Finding a willing seller was only one part of the process. Millions of dollars had to be assembled, different organisations had to coordinate their contributions, and the ecological value of the land had to be weighed against competing possibilities for its future.Reportedly, a federal grant helped move the proposal forward. The US Fish and Wildlife Service provided $660,000, while the state contributed another $165,000. The largest contribution, $1.236 million, came through California's Wildlife Conservation Board using funds from a statewide bond approved by voters in 2002.The Nature Conservancy put $639,000 of its own funds into the purchase. Escrow finally closed on June 30, 2003.How one purchase could protect more Ramona grasslandsThe $2.7 million transaction protected 417 acres, but conservation groups were thinking beyond that single purchase.At the time, the Ramona grasslands covered roughly 8,000 acres and contained several large privately held parcels. The Cagney property helped connect existing conservation plans and offered a possible route towards a larger protected landscape.The Wildlife Research Institute, which owned 10 acres beside the southwest corner of the new preserve, intended to continue working towards protecting more of the grasslands. Its researchers had been documenting the area's wildlife and habitat for years.For them, the acquisition was a beginning rather than an endpoint.The broader conservation ambition was to keep substantial parts of the grassland intact while finding ways for development and habitat protection to coexist elsewhere. That was important in a county where coastal, mountain and desert environments meet, producing an unusually varied collection of habitats.What remained from the old ranchThe 417 acres carried a family name linked to one of Hollywood's most recognisable actors, but the property's significance eventually came from something far removed from the film industry.Pieces of the original Cagney holding had disappeared over the decades as land changed hands. The remaining parcel was the part that could still make a difference to the surrounding ecosystem.In 2003, the Nature Conservancy described it as one of the last remnants of grassland habitat in coastal Southern California. The purchase kept that section from following the same path as many other flat, developable pieces of the region.The landscape itself had not changed overnight. There was no new monument or dramatic transformation when the sale closed. articles.title: Thames Hospice site featured in Ted Lasso's new season
articles.summary: Part of the hospice's site was used for filming in September for the show's fourth season.
articles.body:
A Berkshire hospice took centre stage in hit show Ted Lasso after an unused wing was transformed into a film set.

Thames Hospice's Otter Wing in Maidenhead was used by the cast and crew of the Emmy-winning programme, which follows the fortunes of the fictional AFC Richmond, when filming took place last September.

Chief executive Rachael de Caux said hiring out the space is an important revenue stream for the hospice, which needs £44,000 a day to provide its services.

She said everyone involved in filming the show's fourth season was "very humble, down to earth, [with] absolutely no diva-like behaviour at all".

She added: "It was exciting and it also means that the hospice is a living, breathing place. It's a happy place where sad things happen but actually life does go on through it.

"[The cast and crew] were very professional, very considerate. We're able to isolate the wing they were using so there was very little impact to the rest of our staff and users."

She said parts of the wing were temporarily transformed by the show's production crew.

"It's really odd when you're so used to what your ward looks like and the amazing crew come in and dress it in a day and a half. So even though you know you're in your own clinical space, it's unrecognisable," de Caux added.

The hospice said it has plans to reuse the Otter Wing for clinical use, with more details expected to be released later this year.

Listen to the latest news from Berkshire

A small elephant sculpture was painted in AFC Richmond's blue and red and signed by the show's stars including Jason Sudeikis and Hannah Waddingham during filming.

It will be auctioned off alongside other items in October as part of the hospice's Trunks Across the Thames appeal .

Thirty elephant sculptures will remain in place across Windsor and Slough until 13 September and will then be sold off to raise funds the following month.

articles.title: What will you tell your grandchildren about the summer of '26?
articles.summary: It has been a summer of broken records, wildfires and hosepipe bans across the South.
articles.body:
For decades, 1976 has been the benchmark for hot summers in the UK.

But half a century later, has 2026 now claimed that position?

It has been a summer of broken records, wildfires and hosepipe bans across the South.

As it draws to a close, we look back on some of the moments that will be talked about for years to come.

By mid-July, Reading University's Atmospheric Observatory said the year had already seen more days above 30C than the whole of 1976, with 15 by that point, compared with 14.

It also became the first year on record to reach 35C in May, June and July.

On 24 June, Gosport in Hampshire reached 36.1C, breaking the UK's June record , which had stood at 35.6C since 1976.

That original record was set at Mayflower Park in Southampton on 28 June 1976 - meaning the 50-year-old record fell to a spot on the same stretch of Hampshire coastline.

The new record was not to last. It was broken again the following day in Somerset, and again the day after in Norfolk, where temperatures eventually peaked at 37.7C - the hottest June day ever recorded in the UK.

Another record fell when Kew Gardens broke the UK's May record twice in two days, and by 9 July, the country had already recorded eight days above 34C - more than any year on record, including 1976.

Listen to the latest news from Oxfordshire

The summer of 2026 will also be remembered as a summer of wildfires.

Fires broke out across England as the heat and lack of rain left swathes of countryside tinder-dry.

Concern over the fires came to a head on 14 August when the government issued an emergency alert to phones across England and Wales, warning of the risk and imposing a temporary ban on the sale of disposable barbecues.

Few places in the region felt that impact more than the New Forest.

On 9 August, a van fire on the A31 near Ringwood spread into the heathland and ancient woodland of the national park.

By the time fire crews finally left the scene two weeks later, more than a square kilometre had burned.

At its height, the blaze required firefighters from across the country and the A31 itself - a main route between Southampton and Bournemouth - stayed closed for more than a week, causing major disruption.

Forestry England said the fire had destroyed trees along with rare heathland and wildlife, warning it would take decades for the environment to fully recover.

In Oxfordshire, a large fire broke out at a landfill site near Didcot in August, sending a thick plume of smoke across the area and forcing nearby residents indoors.

Fire crews in Berkshire said 2026 was on course to be worse than 2022 , with incidents up in both number and scale.

Among those was a blaze in Upper Basildon believed to have started when a combine harvester's blade struck a flint.

And in Dorset, the pressure became so intense that a major incident was declared on 13 August as crews battled a high number of fires simultaneously, including one which destroyed a barn at East Lulworth, believed to have been started deliberately.

Fires were not the only consequence of the extremely dry weather.

By mid-summer, hosepipe bans had spread across almost the entire region.

Southern Water was the first to act, banning hosepipes across Hampshire and the Isle of Wight from 10 July.

Thames Water followed on 23 July , restricting customers across Oxfordshire and parts of Berkshire, while South East Water brought in its own ban covering Hampshire and Berkshire from 25 July.

On 29 July, the Environment Agency formally declared a drought across parts of the region, including Hampshire and the Isle of Wight and the Thames Valley.

Rivers ran at some of their lowest levels on record and reservoir storage fell well below average for the time of year.

One of the most striking moments came on 18 August, when Wessex Water introduced its first hosepipe ban in 50 years , covering parts of Dorset and Hampshire.

The company said it was the first time restrictions had been needed in the area since the drought of 1976.

For thousands of families, the summer of 2026 will be remembered as the summer school finished early.

At the peak of the June heatwave, about 200 schools across the region announced closures or reduced hours, with some shutting entirely and others offering early collection as temperatures topped 36C.

In Oxfordshire, about 140 schools faced disruption, while dozens more closed or cut their hours across West Berkshire.

On the Isle of Wight, three secondary schools closed or partially closed over consecutive days as the island came under a red heat-health alert.

Not every council took the same approach. In Dorset, most schools stayed open throughout, with the local council advising headteachers that school was often the safest place for children to be.

Greggs closed stores across the country , including in Gosport and Wantage, to "protect its customers and colleagues" during the worst of the heat.

Rail operators cut services and warned of longer journey times, while councils in Reading and Slough opened "cool spaces" for anyone struggling to stay comfortable at home.

An ice rink in Slough saw a rush of regulars who said it was the best place in town to exercise without overheating.

While an outdoor pool in Abingdon, Oxfordshire, reopened almost a month early after pressure from residents.

Behind the record-breaking numbers, the heat put real strain on the region's emergency and health services.

University Hospital Southampton NHS Foundation Trust declared a critical incident as its buildings struggled to cope with the heat.

South Central Ambulance Service also declared a critical incident due to an "unprecedented" level of calls, driven largely by dehydration and collapses among elderly people.

South Western Ambulance Service had its busiest day on record , managing over 4,300 incidents in a single day - a rise of more than a third on typical demand.

A third service, South East Coast Ambulance Service, covering north-east Hampshire, also declared a critical incident , asking the public to call 999 only in life-threatening emergencies.

According to UKHSA, an estimated 2,877 people died from heat-related causes in England during the May and June heatwaves.

A separate rapid analysis by the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, Imperial College London and the Met Office found that climate change was responsible for around 42% of those deaths.

It also added 3C to 4C to daytime temperatures that would not have been reached in a world without human-caused global warming.

Liz Bentley, chief executive of the Reading-based Royal Meteorological Society, said summers were only going to become hotter and drier - and that what the region had just lived through was "kind of the new norm for us in the UK".

She warned that if a dry autumn and winter followed, the region could face even greater pressure on its water supplies next year - and that wildfires, once a rarity in the UK, were now one of the fastest-growing risks in the country.

So will the summer of 2026 really prove to be the new benchmark - or just the one that set the bar for those to come?

articles.title: Heavy rain creates 'another challenge' for Holme Fen crews
articles.summary: Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service thank local farmers and organisations for their help.
articles.body:
A fire service has said recent spells of heavy rain have created "another challenge" for crews tackling a peatland fire which has been burning for nearly a month.

Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service thanked local farmers and organisations for helping them control the blaze at Holme Fen Nature Reserve, near Peterborough, which started on 8 August.

A spokesperson for the service said: "Whilst the rainfall has raised the moisture content of the peat, it is impacting the ability for heavy machinery to be used to clear the area."

Yellow weather warnings for lightning and heavy rain were issued for parts of the region last week, resulting in flash floods in Peterborough .

A spokesperson said the rain created "another challenge for crews responding".

They added: "Despite the heavy rainfall over the last day or so, the risk remains for wildfires" after "such a long, dry prolonged period".

"We'd still urge people to be extra careful and follow our safety advice," they added.

The fire service said it was "regularly reviewing" the situation at the site, with firefighters expected to continue in the area until September.

The fire service thanked everyone who helped with the response, including local farmers.

On Facebook it said: "We were inundated with offers of help in the initial stages and the willingness from the local farmers to do all they could to support our firefighting tactics was very much appreciated."

It also thanked multiple organisations for their involvement as part of the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Local Resilience Forum.

articles.title: Farmers grieving over bluetongue urged to talk
articles.summary: Bluetongue has hit farmers hard and they have dreaded seeing the impact on their livestock.
articles.body:
Farmers and support workers say bluetongue has hit agriculture hard and fear it will have a "lasting impact".

South-west England has been particularly badly affected by the virus. Farmers who have lost animals to the virus are feeling "a tremendous sense of grief", said Andy Jerrard, the Methodist Church's rural support worker.

Jerry Sanders-Carr, who runs Exe Valley Lamb, near Exeter, and has lost 15% of his sheep to bluetongue said farmers were offering each other support.

He said: "Talking to some of the guys who've been going out picking up large numbers of dead animals every morning, some of these guys I'm sure there's going to be a lasting impact on them."

How bluetongue virus exploded in the South West

Sanders-Carr said: "I know talking to people who have experienced foot-and-mouth they came out of it with PTSD-type symptoms and I wouldn't be surprised if that some guys who've had it far worse than I've had it will be materially affected mentally."

He has vaccinated just under 700 sheep at a cost of £15,000 and said "had a huge impact" but it had been distressing at the height of the virus on his farm.

Bluetongue can make sheep and cattle lethargic and lame, it can cause birth defects or spontaneous abortions and it can be fatal and is spread by midges.

Sanders-Carr said: "During the peaks of it when we were going out in the morning and treating 40 plus animals that were showing symptoms it was horrendous.

"You didn't want to go out and find sick animals, but you had no choice you've got to get out there and treat them, it was incredibly stressful."

If you or someone you know is affected by this subject and is in need of support, you can find more information at the BBC Action Line .

There were 670 places in the UK with recorded cases of bluetongue by Wednesday 26 August, including 332 in Devon and 110 in Cornwall, according to government figures.

Sanders-Carr said he was getting messages of support from all over the country and farmers have been sharing experience and guidance.

"I've never had so many WhatsApp messages and phone calls from farmers that I maybe only speak to once or twice a year but we've speaking almost weekly in some cases," he said.

Rural support worker Jerrard, who is based in Crediton, said it has had a huge impact of farmers at affected farms in west Somerset, Devon and north-east Cornwall.

He said: "There's a tremendous sense of grief, I think, because these folks are entrusted with animals for their lifetime and there is a sense of having let the animals down by seeing them ill, and that is emotionally exhausting."

Jerrard added farmers have also treated animals "they thought would survive and didn't" and added "seeing animals suffering is hard for them to bear".

He said: "To say they are on their knees is an understatement, a lot of them are on their backs."

Jerrard said the heat had added to the pressure, as farmers were going round inspecting their animals and having to catch them and inject them in heatwave conditions, which had been exhausting.

He said farmers were supporting each other and although they were robust they could be "quite vulnerable".

The rural support worker added: "There are a lot who went through foot-and-mouth who have said this is as bad.

"When something like this hits, then it hurts."

He said farmers were also faced with worries about the impact of bluetongue on animals' fertility next spring.

Cornish farmer Luke Thomas represents Cornwall on the National Farmers' Union livestock board and lost 40 sheep to bluetongue with some lambs orphaned.

He said: "I think people are pretty demoralised, along with the long spell of dry weather.

"Farmers are facing a lot of risk. This summer has exposed the fact that we're so open to risk."

The experience is going to make him change the way he farms, Thomas said.

He explained that his farm had lambs in the summer and feared that had made the flock "more vulnerable" with sheep feeding two lambs the "most badly affected".

Bluetongue has also affected the fertility of a bull and he had to buy in another, which was an "additional expense".

Thomas said one positive was that farmers were talking to each other with a culture "where it's actually ok to talk about how you're feeling".

He added: "I think it takes practice and the more we learn to do it and the more we learn to encourage it, that can only be good."

articles.title: Global coral reef coverage risks irreversible decline, new report warns
articles.summary: Coral reefs make up just 1 percent of ocean coverage, but host a quarter of all life in the sea.
articles.body:
Coral reefs are experiencing bleaching events so frequently that they no longer have time to recover before the next one strikes, scientists have warned.

Global coral cover is now well below ⁠normal levels and at risk of irreversible decline, the Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network (GCRMN) said in a report released on Monday.

“If we give them enough time, they ‌have the capacity to recover,” lead author Manuel Gonzalez Rivero said. “But we haven’t seen that amount of time being allowed. In fact, the frequency of those bleaching events has pretty much doubled.”

Bleaching occurs when corals expel the colourful algae living in their tissues. Without this algae, they become vulnerable to starvation and disease. Bleached coral are not dead, but they need time in cooler water to recover.

“We had 40 years of coral cover around the world that had remained relatively unchanged until 2010,” said Gonzalez Rivero, a scientist at the Australian Institute of Marine Science. “Since 2010, there has ⁠been a very steep change.”

The latest bleaching in 2023 was the most extensive on record, impacting 77 percent of the world’s coral reef areas.

Rivero warned that another such event is “very likely” this year given elevated temperatures globally.

Coral reefs are critical barometers for global ocean health, supporting more than 25 percent of all marine life despite covering less than 1 percent of the ocean floor.

The GCRMN’s warning came as organisers of the annual Pacific Islands Forum announced that at least five leaders of the 18-nation group will skip the group’s summit.

The forum has been touted for decades as a symbol of regional unity, and is used to discuss pressing matters facing Pacific states, including climate change and ocean health.

articles.title: Burst pipes: Why heatwaves are putting pressure on water networks
articles.summary: The record-breaking summer has led to hosepipe bans, burst mains and supply issues across the West.
articles.body:
Burst water mains, dwindling supplies and hosepipe bans across the West of England are just a few issues caused by this year's scorching summer.

On 18 August, a major road was closed in Cheltenham after a burst main sent a "raging river" down the street , threatening to flood residents' homes.

Two days later, a burst main on the edge of Bristol impacted nearly 1,500 homes, severing the water supply for much of the day.

Water companies said they were continually repairing leaks and replacing degrading pipes but, as climate change brings more extreme weather, experts are calling for renewed infrastructure and a more resilient, sustainable approach.

When the ground heats up, it expands and moves - putting strain on underground pipes which are already under pressure, causing them to buckle and split.

Richard Stanbrook, a director at Bristol Water, said: "It's becoming a phenomenon that only used to happened in the winter but it's now happening in the summer because the ground dries out and moves.

"That challenges our pipes because they are more rigid than the ground.

"It's a disaster if we don't get on top of it - but we are very much aware of it."

Burst pipes are much more common in older water networks because ageing materials lose their strength and crack easily, according to Bristol Water.

Some of the company's original infrastructure from 1846 still remains in active use today, including the 11-mile (17km) aqueduct carrying water from the Mendips.

A spokesperson said the prolonged period of hot and dry weather experienced this summer had "placed significant pressure on the network".

The number of bursts increased by 109% between June and July this year, the spokesperson said.

"In response, we have proactively increased our leak detection activities and expanded our repair teams by 55% to accelerate repairs and minimise disruption to customers."

The company said it continued to invest in technology, data-driven insights and improvement programmes, alongside targeted mains replacement and network upgrades.

Dr Francesca Pianosi, associate professor in water and environmental engineering at the University of Bristol, said most UK water networks are simply outdated.

"[They] were built long ago when climate conditions were different from what we are experiencing today, and will likely experience in the future," she said.

In 2018, the National Infrastructure Commission, which advises the government on long-term infrastructure needs, published a report on "preparing for a drier future" .

It recommended reducing leakage, building new supply infrastructure and reducing household demand to improve resilience during periods of drought.

"All those recommendations still hold true and, if anything, are even more urgent as changes in climate seem to be happening faster than anticipated," Pianosi said.

Pianosi described how climate projections were already being used to understand future water balances and "identify where gaps may emerge" between long-term water demand and supply.

However, she noted that investment in infrastructure - alongside variations in geology, soil and land use - meant that future water availability would be difficult to predict.

She suggested issues caused by urban expansion could be "significantly mitigated" by opting for water-saving technology, like rain harvesting or dual supply systems.

"Quantifying how exactly changes in precipitation and temperature translate into changes in demand and supply remains very difficult, as many other hard-to-predict factors affect these relationships," she said.

On 18 August, Wessex Water announced its first hosepipe ban in 50 years as demand surged to 400 million litres per day - 30% above average for the time of year.

The utility company's reservoirs have fallen to 47% capacity following the driest spring and summer on record, while Bristol Water's reservoirs are only 55% full.

Bristol Water also imposed a hosepipe ban after the Environment Agency issued a drought order to protect the River Severn's resources.

Elsewhere in the region, Thames Water - which supplies parts of Wiltshire and Gloucestershire - issued its hosepipe ban on 23 July and South West Water's ban started on 8 August , covering parts of south Somerset.

Wessex Water said about £12m was spent each year on renewing its 7,558-mile (12,163 km) network and maintaining facilities which help store and move water around the region.

It said overall leakage rates had reduced by 60% in the past 30 years.

A spokesperson said: "With an ever-changing climate and growing population, we have a water resources management plan which ensures we're already taking further steps to meet our customers' demand from now to 2080."

While Bristol Water acknowledged performance in 2023-24 and 2024-25 was impacted by "weather extremes", it assured it was taking steps to "strengthen its network and adapt to changing conditions".

"Between April 2024 and March 2025, we successfully repaired 15,637 leaks across our network - reflecting our continued commitment to reducing water loss and improving service reliability," it said.

Since April 2025, Thames Water has also replaced more than 62 miles (100km) of ageing water mains as part of the company's biggest upgrade to its network in 150 years.

A spokesperson for the company said it plans to invest £3.3 billion before 2030 to help reduce leakage and improve long-term resilience.

articles.title: Essex gets £8m in 4 years from TV and film shoots
articles.summary: The total is boosted by a recent shoot in the county featuring Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock.
articles.body:
When Practical Magic 2 spent a chunk of its Hollywood budget in Essex, it meant film and TV spending across the county had reached almost £8m in just under four years.

Epping Ongar Railway received "quite a high figure" for the use of its 1960s carriages for a scene with Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman.

That brought the total estimated spend to approximately £7.8m since the 2022-23 financial year, according to the Essex Film Office, a specialist unit that acts as the main point of contact for film and TV productions.

The county's multi-million economic boost has benefited landowners, caterers, actors, extras and local businesses.

Beacon Hill Fort in Harwich has been a coastal defence site since Henry VIII and was used during World War One and World War Two.

Owner Barry Sharp said he would never charge visitors - donations and filming gigs were "the only way we survive".

The 75-year-old told the BBC that the site had started off "a bit camouflaged" from the outside world.

Sharp said his only revenue came from donations, "lots of ghost hunters" and camera clubs.

"They come from all around the country," he added.

But when film producers called, including the team that made Winnie The Pooh: Blood and Honey , he could earn about £6,000 a week.

Sharp said it was "unbelievable" for the fort, and helped maintain it.

He said he was so grateful to crews that he liked looking after them.

"When they spend the day, I like to feed them," he said.

Safe Fire Protection (SFP) in Rayleigh generates "about £5,000" a year for the work it does on film and TV sets.

Owner Jay Leslie, 35, said he worked regularly with ITV's The Bill.

SFP assesses locations for any dangers and gives advice.

He said: "If they're blowing something up, perhaps, you need a couple of fire engines here. But obviously, that's not something that the county fire and rescue services would go out for.

"They can't sit on stage at the film scene all day."

He said film and TV was a "very small segment" of their turnover, but he had the capacity to help more studios.

Sarah Hardy is a food artist from Sible Hedingham whose first gig was making a cake for Channel 4's comedy series Peep Show.

Since then, she has made giant strawberries for Wuthering Heights and beetles for Frankenstein , but credits her success to simple word of mouth.

"All that's happened, just to unglamorise it, is that a couple of people have got me in their address book.

"You need to put a premium on the work because they also require it incredibly quickly. You drop everything to work for them and they have the budget."

"It's really exciting... I get to be part of something else, part of a bigger thing, but I think it bodes really well for Essex."

A Southend-on-Sea-based company stores valuable props for film and TV productions.

Michelle French, a co-founder of CAMA Asset Store, described the scale of film production spending in Essex as "fantastic news".

"In simple terms, we take the props, sets and costumes from film and TV productions and store, track and reuse them so nothing valuable goes to waste.

"We actually started out working with corporate clients, but film and TV now makes up around 90% of what we do."

She added that it gave "beautiful set pieces and costumes a second life rather than sending them to the skip".
